body: The common thread is that being right is not the point. Pros focus on payoff asymmetry and sizing (Druckenmiller/Soros), on how their view differs from what is already priced in (Marks's second-level thinking, Steinhardt), and on feedback loops between price and fundamentals (Soros). Systematic edges like the magic formula work *because* they are painful to hold.

body: `insight:balance-sheet-survives-cycle` · confidence: unverified Leverage taken on in an upcycle was the common thread in every big Indian sector wipeout. Infrastructure and EPC in 2007–12 (Lanco, GVK, Punj Lloyd, Gammon) used debt plus aggressive bids. Thermal IPPs in 2010–13 had untied PPAs and imported coal. Steel in 2011–16 (Bhushan, Essar, Monnet) ended in IBC. Real estate in 2008–19 (Unitech, Jaypee) diverted customer advances. NBFCs in 2018–19 (IL&FS, DHFL) borrowed short to lend long. Private banks in 2018–20 (Yes Bank) grew loans ahead of deposits. Retail in 2019–20 (Future Group) expanded on debt. The survivors and compounders entered the downturn with net cash or low leverage and gained share when weak players exited: UltraTech and Shree in cement, JSW after its 2016 recovery, HDFC Bank and Kotak in 2008 and 2018, Bajaj Finance after 2008, Radico through FY17–21 deleveraging (D/E 0.77 to 0.15). Sector-specific balance-sheet tests: lenders on deposit/CASA franchise and ALM; cyclicals on net debt/EBITDA under 2x at mid-cycle margins; EPC on working capital and receivables over a year; developers on net debt against annual collections; utilities on discom receivables. Lesson: in cyclical and financial sectors, screen out stretched balance sheets first, then pick on growth. **lesson:** Survive first: screen leverage and funding structure before growth; downturn share gains build the next decade's winners. **examples:** Lanco/GVK 2012; Bhushan/Essar IBC; Unitech/Jaypee; IL&FS/DHFL 2018–19; Yes Bank 2020; Future Group 2020 Sources: [1](https://ticker.finology.in/discover/market-update/hdfc-bank-q2-fy27-results-analysis) · [2](https://www.newkerala.com/news/a/hfcs-emerge-stronger-after-fy26-stress-asset-quality-215.htm) Links: similar_to `insight:avoid-ruin`, illustrates `case_study:radico-khaitan`, about `insight:disqualifiers`

`insight:buffett-conglomerate-chain-letter-2014` | confidence: verified | date: 2015-02-27

2014 letter, 'Berkshire Today': 'Conglomerates ... have a terrible reputation with investors. And they richly deserve it.' The late-1960s drill: 'By personality, promotion or dubious accounting - and often by all three - these managers drove a fledgling conglomerate's stock to, say, 20 times earnings and then issued shares as fast as possible to acquire another business selling at ten-or-so times earnings. They immediately applied "pooling" accounting to the acquisition, which - with not a dime's worth of change in the underlying businesses - automatically increased per-share earnings, and used the rise as proof of managerial genius.' The game needs an ever-rising stock price and ends when it stops. Same letter credits Munger's blueprint: 'Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices.' Berkshire's own rule (1983/1989): issue stock only 'when we receive as much in intrinsic business value as we give.' Actionable red flag for Indian markets: serial acquirers or roll-ups paying with richly valued paper or QIP money, rising EPS mostly from acquisitions, goodwill growing faster than operating cash flow, frequent restatements/segment changes. Test: organic growth and cash conversion excluding acquisitions.

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2014ltr.pdf
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1983.html

- **Pay:** SBC is a major cost in the US.

- **Efficiency:** US large caps are very efficient, so any edge is more plausible in under-covered small caps and in forensic filing work.
- **Data:** XBRL coverage, full-text search and coded 8-K items make systematic screening much cheaper than in India.

body:
CIL reports **one** segment ("Engines"). The best public handle on line margins is the **AGM-notice RPT pricing table** `[AR26 AGM notice, item 10 annex]`. Copied verbatim:
- **Sales to group companies (CL UK, TCPL, CTIPL, CMI):** "manufactured engines and gensets: **cost plus at least 11% mark-up**; manufactured components and spares: cost plus 14% mark-up / prices charged to third-party dealers".
- **Purchases from CTIPL:** "engines for manufacturing – **cost plus 11%** markup; turbochargers… third-party pricing; components and spares for distribution – cost plus 5%". From TCPL: "cost plus profit margins approved by TCPL Board… uniform to JV partners".
- **Royalty to CMI: "4% of eligible sales."** Agreement "for a period of three years **up to March 31, 2027**… usually renewed".

**What this implies** [EST, method shown, confidence unverified]:
- **Exports are mostly to the group at cost +11%.** Outside-India revenue was ₹2,007 cr `[AR26 n.26]`. Sales to Cummins Ltd UK alone were ₹1,018 cr (51% of exports), and "others" group sales were ₹607 cr. So roughly **50–80% of exports are priced at cost +11%**. A cost-plus-11% sale earns ~10% on sales before CIL's own overheads, against the company's 21% EBITDA. **Exports are structurally the lowest-margin line, and a weak rupee does not flow through in full:** the mark-up is on cost, not on market price.
- **Back-solving domestic margin.** If ~₹2,000 cr of exports earn ~10% [EST], domestic earns ≈ (2,595 − 200) ÷ 10,143 ≈ **23.6% EBITDA** [EST]. Distribution (parts and service) is normally the richest line at Cummins globally, so domestic power gen is probably below 23.6% and distribution above. *Unverified; no line P&L is disclosed.*
- **The FY27 approvals show how far management expects group trade to grow** (ceilings, not forecasts): sales to CL UK up to ₹1,975 cr (FY26 actual ₹1,018 cr); purchases from TCPL ₹2,231 cr (actual ₹1,399 cr), from CTIPL ₹2,074 cr (actual ₹1,317 cr), from CMI ₹779 cr; CMI "other RPTs" ₹619 cr, raised by ₹11 cr in Nov-2026 for the new MD's seconded cost `[PB-Nov26]`.
